about: THE SHIP ROSTER, 793-1066: the twenty craft a house can own, in the order a house climbs through them (Design/ships_roster.md is the one-page reading). Each entry is a full class in the format of Data/ship_classes_793.json (same field names, same units: see that file's units), so it can be merged straight into its classes. in_class_table = true: the id is already a row there, and changed_from_table lists every number that differs here and why (take them or leave them one by one). in_class_table = false: a new row. After the class fields come the roster fields (units below). Evidence is taken from Design/content/ships.md (its source keys in square brackets) and from the class table; nothing was opened again for this file. (D) = derived or judged by me from the numbers named; (?) = not checked against a source. No sale price for any merchant ship of these years survives: every cost_d is derived (ships.md 8.2) and set against the money scale of Design/content/CHAINS.md (a small boat about 600 d, a sea-going trader several thousand).

units.from, to: the years a house can have her new. Real years here (793 = from the start, 1066 = to the end); the class table writes 0 for both, which means the same
units.built_at: port ids of Data/ports_793.json where she is built to order or had second-hand. built_at_note says when a yard falls away or opens (Dorestad is raided from 834 and gone after 863)
units.cost_d: pennies, new, with her gear (oars, rope, an anchor, a sail). Second-hand: half at ten to fifteen years old, a quarter at twenty (ships.md 8.2)
units.build_days: days from the order to the launch
units.crew_min: the fewest men who can work her at all (slower, no rowing watch, more risk)
units.crew_full: the men she is meant to have. Her class field crew is the usual number, between the two
units.cargo_kg: cargo beyond crew and gear, at crew_full; always cargo_t x 1000
units.can_go: four waters, each yes, limited or no. river = above the tide, upstream; flats = tidal flats and bars (the Wadden, the Almere shore, a drying creek); coast = within a day of land; open_sea = a crossing out of sight of land. can_go_note says what limited means for her
units.upkeep_d_a_year: pennies a year for tar, rivets, rope and mending, with no wages or food in it. Rule (D): 2.5 per cent of cost_d for keel ships, 4 per cent for river craft (moss and laths every year, a short life); the hide boat 10 d for hides and grease
units.life_years: years before she is worth only her timber (ships.md 7.3): 25 to 30 for a clinker ship, 10 for a barge. A refit of the rivets in year 15 costs a tenth of cost_d (D)
units.how_had: bought = any house with the silver and the standing; reward = only by the flag unlock_flag (a chain, a riddle, a service); both = bought, and also given as a reward
units.unlock_flag: the flag of Design/content/CHAINS.md that gives the right to her or the hull itself
units.rung: her step on the ladder of Design/ships_roster.md: 1 boat, 2 bigger boat or river craft, 3 the ship, 4 the knarr, 5 the great ship; 0 = off the ladder (a side road or a reward)
units.what_it_is, why_want_it: plain words for a designer, not text for the player (the user writes that)

rules: A ship is offered only when year >= from, and new only while year <= to. A player who is rich in 810 is offered more hulls, never a knarr (ships.md 10).
River and sea are two fleets: flat craft need oak and no iron; keel ships need iron, wool and a winter. The old boat is kept as the lighter (research_scale_to_fleets.md 4.7, you always have a boat).
A knarr or the great ship cannot be beached laden: she needs a jetty or a towed boat (west_small_boat or norse_small_boat as her boat).

Prices that differ from story/unlocks_793.json as it stands: logboat_expanded 300 (there 250), river_barge 600 (there 900), north_sea_merchant_ship 3000 (there 2400), hedeby_great_ship 15000 (there 12000). Years that differ: knarr from 900 at the Norse yards (there 1000), baltic_coastal_boat to 1066 (there 850), coaster_minster_ship can also be bought (there only lent by a minster, to 870). Each is argued in its entry; one of the two files should give way.

ships.name: Gislinge boat (the house boat)
ships.period_name: batr; a six-oar boat, ON sexaeringr (?) (the Norse names are attested only later, LATER)
evidence: Viking Ship Museum, the Gislinge boat: built about 1130, 7.7 m; the replica Langoe 7.7 x 1.64 x 0.25 m, sail 10 m2, six oars, two to four men, put at 6 kn under sail [VSM-Lang] [VSM-Gis]
For 793 the same kind of boat is vouched for by the Kvalsund boat (9.5 m, 780-800) [WP-Kval] and by iron rivets in the Frisian terps, 400-800 [BJM]
Kapman ShipClass Gislinge_WorkingBoat.asset: 4.8 kn on the beam at 8 m/s, rowing 3.5 kn, closest to wind 58
ships.look: Slender double-ended clinker boat, low sheer, gently raised stems; 3 pairs of oars; a short mast amidships with a small square sail. The existing Gislinge model.
uncertain: LATER: built about 1130, a stand-in for the working boats of 793
mast and sail reconstructed: none survived (?)
cargo: the museum tonne is four men and ten sheep, so it counts the men; 660 kg beside four men is the project figure (BRIEF.md)
ships.built_at_note: any landing with a wright; Dorestad until 863
ships.can_go_note: open sea in settled weather only: 34 cm of freeboard. Her crew drag her over a bar. Upstream she gains little on a strong current under oars.
ships.what_it_is: A small open clinker boat with six oars and one square sail, worked by four men. She carries about two thirds of a ton: wine by the cask, querns by the pair.
ships.why_want_it: She is the start: the one hull that goes everywhere a little, up a creek, over the flats and along the coast.
ships.source: ships.md 4.3, 5.1, 7.2, 8.2; ship_classes_793.json gislinge; price as CHAINS.md (bare boat 300 to 450 d (D), 600 d with her gear)
judged: build_days 45: a wright and three men, six to eight weeks (D); unlocks_793.json gives 120 (ordered before Candlemas, ready at Easter) and town_actions gives 30
crew_min 2 from the museum range
changed_from_table: cargo_t 0.9 -> 0.66 (BRIEF.md; the museum tonne counts the men)
uses: trade_long added, she is the player's trading boat

ships.name: Flat-bottomed plank river barge, 15 m, towed upstream
ships.period_name: Latin navis (?); German Prahm (modern term)
ships.cultures_note: frankish: Rhineland, Ripuaria; frisian: on the Rhine; continental_saxon: Weser
ships.sail: towing mast; rarely a small sail before the wind (?)
ships.crew_range: 2-3 aboard + 3-6 hauling on the bank upstream
evidence: Krefeld-Gellep III (Rhine), 8th c: 15.2 m; load 6,961 kg; mast step read as a towing mast (class table)
Kalkar-Niedermormter, about 802: sank with a cargo of tuff stone, at least 4.5 t [BJM]
Karl (Bremen, Weser), after 808: 16-20 x 2.5-3 m (class table)
Wandalbert, Miracles of St Goar (about 839): a Frisian's ship hauled up the Rhine by rope from the bank, as is customary (class table)
ships.look: Long, low and box-like; flat raked ends, no stem posts; a short sturdy towing mast a quarter of the length from the bow; cargo heaped amidships; a steering oar aft.
uncertain: drift speed is an estimate (?)
Seine and Loire hulls (?): no find

ships.what_it_is: A flat box of oak planks caulked with moss, with no iron in her, hauled upstream by men on the bank. Seven tons of stone, grain or wine with three men aboard.
ships.why_want_it: Bulk: she carries what ten boats carry, at the lowest price for each ton of any hull, but only where the river goes.
judged: cost 600 d (D): ships.md puts a 20 m barge at 550 to 800 d, so the 15 m one sits at the low end; unlocks_793.json has 900
life 10 years: the Tiel barges [BJM]

ships.name: Large river barge, 20 m (from about 826)
ships.period_name: Latin navis (?); the name is lost: call her a flat boat or a river ship
ships.cultures_note: the Rhine, the Kromme Rijn, the Vecht, the IJssel
ships.crew_range: 2-4 aboard + 6-10 hauling on the bank upstream
evidence: Cothen: after about 826, about 20 x 2.5-4 x 1.25 m, in the bed of the old Rhine a few km below Dorestad [BJM]
Vleuten 2: about 959, about 20 x 3.5 m, side 1.15 m high; no iron in her at all; Ardennes oak; a wooden peg in the side as a thole [BJM]
Utrecht 3: after about 1004, 23 x 3.3-4 m, nearly complete [BJM]
Tiel I and II (about 990-1014): about ten years afloat, then built into the harbour front [BJM]
ships.look: The 15 m barge drawn longer: a low oak box with raked ends that lands on a sloping bank; a towing mast forward; a long heap of cargo.
uncertain: cargo 15 to 25 t (D): 20 x 3.5 x 0.6 m of draught, a box four-fifths full, less 6 to 8 t of hull
the hauling gang's size (D)
ships.built_at_note: Dorestad until 863; after it Traiectum, Daventre and the Rhine towns. Between 950 and 1050 her oak comes from the Ardennes [BJM]
ships.can_go_note: the great river only: she draws 0.6 m and needs a gang of six to ten on the bank upstream. Never the sea.
ships.what_it_is: The Rhine barge at the size it reaches after Charlemagne: twenty metres of flat oak, hauled by a gang. She carries fifteen to twenty-five tons with three men aboard.
ships.why_want_it: More than twice the old barge in one hull: whole cargoes of wine in tuns, building stone and grain, which is how a river fleet feeds a sea ship.
judged: cargo 18 t, inside the derived 15 to 25 t
cost 800 d: the top of the derived 550 to 800 d
upstream 10 km a day: the low end of [BJM] for the heavier hull (D)

ships.name: Utrecht ship, 17 m (the river freighter at full size, from about 950)
ships.period_name: none known; perhaps the hulc of the London toll of about 1000 (?), not proved [MASS-Utr]
ships.cultures_note: the Rhine, the Vecht, the Almere; fragments at Antwerp and in London
ships.waters_note: coast: the Almere and inside the Wadden; a short crossing in calm weather at a risk
ships.sail: a small mast a third of the way from the bow: a tow line, perhaps a small sail before the wind (?)
evidence: Utrecht 1: after about 1019 [MASS-Utr] or 997-1027 [nl-Utr]; 17.45 x 3.84 m; about 13 t on 0.7 m of draught; the bottom one oak trunk at least 14 m long, hollowed to 4-6 cm and spread to 2 m; raised with clinker planks on wooden pegs; a small mast step a third of the way from the bow
Utrecht 2, 11th c, 12.8 x 3 m; Zeewolde PZ 49, about 900 [BJM]
Queenhithe, London: fragments of a large Utrecht type, the wood perhaps from the lower Rhine: if so she crossed the sea [BJM]
The inventory judges the type sturdier than the barges and able to manage a short sea crossing [BJM, citing Van de Moortel 2009]
ships.look: A great banana of a hull: a broad log bottom, ends swept high, heavy half-trunk wales along the sides, a small mast well forward. About the largest a logboat could be made.
uncertain: from 950 is a judgment (D): Zeewolde about 900 is the type, the full-size finds are 11th c
sail or tow line only (?)
whether she is the hulk is not known
ships.built_at_note: Tiel is not in ports_793.json; if it is added she is built there too. The oak comes from the Ardennes down the Maas [BJM]
ships.can_go_note: coast: sheltered water. Open sea: one short crossing in calm weather, at a real risk (gale_fragility 0.85). She cannot beat to windward at all.
ships.what_it_is: A single huge oak hollowed, spread and built up into a seventeen-metre freighter with no iron in her hull. Four men take thirteen tons from Cologne to the Almere, hauled up and drifting down.
ships.why_want_it: The river and the sheltered sea in one hull: wine goes from Cologne to the Frisian coast without being moved from a barge to a ship.
judged: cost 1200 d: derived 900 to 1,400 d; finding the tree is the hard part, so the yard may ask the house to bring the oak (D)
build_days 100: six men, three to four months
life 20 years (D): the log bottom is stronger than a planked one

ships.period_name: cog; Frisians are Cokingi in a 9th-century annal; the due cogsculd on the Almere, 10th c [BJM]

ships.crew_range: 5-8 trading; more when she is rowed for the levy (?)
evidence: The words: Frisians called Cokingi (the Annals of St Bertin for 867 (?)); a royal tithe on the Almere called cogsculd, 10th c; Frisian districts owe rowed ships called kogge or heerkogge [BJM]
The angular, straight-ended ship on the Hedeby coins from about 825, which some call the forerunner of the cog [BJM, figure 7]
Iron caulking clamps of the later cog's kind, traced to the Frisian area [de-Kogge]
LATER by a century: the oldest cog found, Kollerup, oak felled about 1150: 20.9 x 4.92 m, draught 1.35 m [de-Kogge]
ships.look: A flat-bottomed hull with straight raked ends and clinker sides, high and boxy beside a keel ship; she sits upright on the sand when the tide leaves her; one mast, a few oars a side.
uncertain: NO HULL OF THESE YEARS IS FOUND: every number here is a reconstruction (D) and should be shown to nobody as fact
from 870 follows the word, not a find
closest_to_wind 75 (D): a flat bottom makes much leeway; she gains 0.5 kn to windward at best (ships.md 5.3)
ships.built_at_note: the Frisian coast and the Almere: Medemblik, Stavoren, Wieringen, Texel [BJM]; only the first is a port id
ships.can_go_note: the flats are what she is for: she loads and unloads aground. River: the great rivers' lower reaches. Open sea: short crossings; she will not work to windward off a lee shore.
ships.what_it_is: The Frisians' own ship as far as words and coins show it: flat-bottomed, straight-ended, clinker-sided, and able to be rowed in the king's service. Six men and eight to fifteen tons, loaded on the bare sand between tides.
ships.why_want_it: Ten tons over the flats: she works the Wadden, the Almere and the Limfjord at any state of tide, where a keel ship must wait for water or a jetty.
judged: everything but the name: size, cargo, speed, price (3,000 to 4,000 d derived)
a good reward: a Frisian district that owes a rowed cog may give the right to build one

ships.name: Small sailing trader with an open hold, 14 m (the Skuldelev 3 kind)
ships.period_name: ON byrdingr (?), skuta (?) (later words)
ships.waters_note: sea: the Danish waters, the Baltic, the Kattegat; river: tidal reaches
evidence: Skuldelev 3, about 1040, Danish oak: 14 x 3.3 x 0.9 m, displaces 9.6 t, carries 4.6 t, sail 45 m2, five oar ports, 5 to 8 men; a deck fore and aft and an open hold amidships [VSM-S3]

Roar Ege trials, 1984-85: about 4 kn over long distances, 8 to 10 kn at the most; six oars give 3.2 kn at the top and 2.0 kept up; 1.7 kn made good to windward in light air; in the open Kattegat water comes in across the gunwale [VSM-Roar] [VSM-Trips]
Roar Ege took 54 m3 of green timber, 1,204 rivets and about 20,000 hours, 5,000 of them for sail and rope [EXARC]
Dorestat-1, sailing from Wijk bij Duurstede since 2021, is a replica of this ship [rodi]
ships.look: A neat oak trader: decked at bow and stern, an open hold between, three oar ports forward and two aft, one mast with a square wool sail.
uncertain: from 900 is a judgment (D): the cargo-only build is not found earlier; the find is about 1040
freeboard and sail_top (D)
ships.can_go_note: river: the tidal reaches. Flats: she takes the ground on her keel, leaning. Open sea: the Baltic and the Kattegat; the North Sea in fair weather only; about 2 m of sea is her limit.
ships.what_it_is: A fourteen-metre ship built only to carry under sail, with decks at the ends and a hold between. Five men take four and a half tons, and they hardly row at all.
ships.why_want_it: A trader's cargo with half the crew of the old Norse ship: the Baltic run pays, because five men eat and not twelve.
judged: cost 2400 d: derived 2,000 to 2,700 d
build_days 150: eight men, a winter

ships.name: Large Slav trading boat, 14 m (the Ralswiek kind)
ships.period_name: none known (?)
ships.cultures_note: slav: Rani of Rugen, Obodrites, Pomeranians
ships.waters_note: sea: the southern Baltic in summer; river: mouths and lagoons
evidence: Ralswiek (Rugen), four boats found 1967-1980 at the trading place, 9th-10th c (?): up to 14 metres long and 3.40 metres wide [de-Rals]
Ralswiek 2: planks pegged with treenails, moss caulking (?); a replica made a trial voyage in 1998 [JSON] (?)
The Slav boat is clinker, double-ended, with a keel, a mast step and a side rudder: a tradition closely related to the Scandinavian [BJM]
ships.look: A broad, low clinker hull with plain stems; rows of wooden peg heads along the seams; one mast; oars along the fore and after parts.
uncertain: cargo 5 to 8 t (D) by size against the Graveney boat
speeds are the 10 m Slav boat's (D)
from 900 (D): the Ralswiek dates were not checked (?)
the Slav ports of the 10th c (Wolin, Ralswiek) are not in ports_793.json
ships.built_at_note: Reric is gone after 808; add Wolin or Ralswiek if they become ports
ships.can_go_note: river mouths and lagoons; the Baltic in summer.
ships.what_it_is: The largest of the Wendish boats: fourteen metres, pegged with wood and caulked with moss, with no iron to buy. Seven men and about six tons.
ships.why_want_it: A sea trader's cargo for half a sea trader's price, for a house with a friend or a factor on the Wendish coast.
judged: cost 1500 d (D): half the western trader, as the 10 m Slav boat is half the coaster
all speeds and the crew

ships.name: Knarr: the sea-going cargo ship, 16 m (from about 900)
ships.period_name: ON knorr; OE cnear by 937 (?); kaupskip (?)
ships.cultures_note: norse yards first; by about 1000 built in the delta and in England (the Tiel keel ship is of English and Ardennes timber)
ships.waters_note: coast and the tidal reaches at high water, with a pilot
evidence: Askekarr (Gota alv), built about 900-920, repaired about 1010: about 16 x 4.6 m, about 20 t, sail about 90 m2, in use at least a hundred years [sv-Ask]
Skuldelev 1, about 1030, Sognefjord pine: 15.84 x 4.8 x 1.0 m; 24 t at a 40 per cent freeboard [CP], the replica about 20 t; sail 90 m2; 2 to 4 oars; 6 to 8 men, 5 at the least [VSM-S1] [WP-Skuld]
Klastad (Vestfold), tree rings 998: 20 to 22 m, lost with whetstone blanks aboard [no-Kla]; the Tiel keel ship, 995-1008 [BJM]

Ottar trials: 5 to 7 kn on average, 10 kn at the most, 1.5 kn under oars; 9.8 kn through the Skagerrak in a gale with waves of 3 to 4 m; across the North Sea only four degrees off course [VSM-Ottar] [VSM-Trips]
Vidfamne (Askekarr replica) needs at least 7 t of ballast when light [sv-Ask]
ships.look: Short, broad and high-sided beside every other ship of her day; decked fore and aft with a deep open hold; one tall mast and a big square sail; almost no oars; a boat towed astern.
uncertain: freeboard, hull_top and sail_top (D)
the name in a Frisian's mouth (?)
ships.built_at_note: 900: the Norse and Danish yards only. From about 1000 also the delta and England (the Tiel ship). Tiel is not in ports_793.json
ships.can_go_note: the open sea and the ocean, in seas of about 4 m. Grounding laden is damage: she lies at a jetty or at anchor and lands her goods by her boat. She needs 7 t of ballast when she sails light, and she cannot be rowed against anything.
ships.what_it_is: The first ship built for nothing but cargo on the open sea: sixteen metres, broad and deep, under ninety square metres of wool. Six to eight men carry twenty tons, and she rides out a gale.
ships.why_want_it: Three times the keel's cargo with the same crew, and the whole North Sea in any sailing weather: York, Norway and Dublin stop being ventures and become routes.
ships.source: ships.md 2.3, 4.15, 5.1, 5.3, 6, 7.2, 8.2, 10, 11.1 (knarr); the id is the one unlocks_793.json already waits for
judged: cost 6000 d: derived 5,300 to 7,600 d, and it is the price in unlocks_793.json
from 900 (Askekarr), not 1000 as in unlocks_793.json; a house may be held to a quarter or half share (ships.md 10: she is bought in shares)
gale_fragility 0.2 (D)

ships.name: The great cargo ship of Hedeby, 22 m (from about 1025)
ships.period_name: ON knorr (?); in an Englishman's mouth about 1000 a keel or a hulk
evidence: Hedeby 3, built at Hedeby about 1025: a sturdily built cargo ship of a type similar to Skuldelev 1 but with a cargo capacity of as much as about 60 tons by the hypothetical reconstruction, about 22 m long and 6.25 m wide [Hed3]; another summary gives 40 to 50 t [CP]
LATER: Lynaes, mid 12th c, at least 60 t; Bergen in the 1240s, over 150 t [CP]
ships.look: A knarr grown huge: very broad, very deep, high sides, one great mast; no oars at all; she lies at a jetty with lighters round her.
uncertain: draught about 1.5 m, crew 8 to 12, speeds and sail area are all (D) or (?)
cargo 50 t stands between the two readings (40 to 50 and up to 60)
ships.built_at_note: Hedeby, where the one find was built. She can lie only where there is a jetty: sliesthorp, lundenwic, eoforwic, ripa, traiectum, birka (D)
ships.can_go_note: open sea in anything a ship can live in. She cannot be rowed or beached: she is warped or towed by her boat, and unloads at a jetty or into lighters.
ships.what_it_is: The largest trader known from the age, built at Hedeby about 1025: twenty-two metres long, over six broad, carrying forty to sixty tons with about ten men. No single house fills her alone.
ships.why_want_it: A whole season's trade in one voyage: fifty tons at the lowest sea price for each ton, for a house with partners, a factor and a jetty at both ends.
ships.source: ships.md 2.3, 4.16, 5.3, 6, 7.2, 8.2, 10, 11.1 (great_cargo_ship); the id is the one unlocks_793.json already waits for
judged: cost 15000 d: derived 13,000 to 20,000 d; unlocks_793.json has 12,000
build_days 360: twenty-five men, a year and more
nearly every number: one find, one hypothetical reconstruction

ships.name: Gaelic currach (hide boat on a wooden frame)
ships.period_name: Latin curuca / curucus; Old Irish curach
evidence: Texts only, no hull: Adomnan, Life of Columba (about 700): hide boats beside wooden boats on Iona (class table)
Dicuil (825), of voyages about 795: to the northern islands in two days and two nights under full sail (class table)
The Voyage of St Brendan (9th-10th c (?)): a mast amidships, a sail, hides tanned with oak bark [WP-Cur]
LATER: Tim Severin's Brendan, 1976-77: 11 m, 49 ox hides, Kerry to Newfoundland in two summers; she would not work to windward (?) [WP-Sev]
ships.look: Light and buoyant: high, gently curved sheer, rounded bow, no keel post; dark hide skin, no planks or rivets; a short mast forward of amidships.
uncertain: sizes and rig (?)
no keel, much leeway: closest_to_wind 75 (?)
ships.can_go_note: open sea, even the ocean, in summer with the wind free; she cannot beat. Light enough to carry up a beach or past a fall.
ships.what_it_is: A boat of ox hides stretched on a lashed wooden frame, greased against the sea. Five men and under a ton, so light that her crew carry her.
ships.why_want_it: She goes where nothing else in the west can land: the island monasteries and surf beaches of the Irish Sea and the Hebrides, and over a portage on her crew's shoulders.
ships.source: ships.md 4.5, 5.3, 6; ship_classes_793.json currach; price and makers as unlocks_793.json (120 d, for a man who has served the house of Hi)
judged: life 8 years and upkeep 10 d a year: hides rot and are replaced (D), no evidence
build_days 20 (D)

ships.period_name: Latin navis; naves of the toll charters
ships.cultures_note: frankish: royal, episcopal and monastic households; frisian: skippers hired (?)
ships.sail: towing mast; a sail before the wind now and then (?)

Charlemagne's charter of 779 for Saint-Germain-des-Pres: its ships on the rivers are free of toll (class table)
Annales regni Francorum 793: Charles goes by boat from Regensburg to the Fossa Carolina (class table)

crew and oars (?)

ships.what_it_is: A lord's river ship with cabins, rowed by eight and hauled upstream. She is lent with her lord's letter for a season, never sold; her lord keeps her up.
ships.why_want_it: She carries people of rank dry and under a lord's freedom from toll: a bishop aboard is worth more than her three tons.

ships.name: Small warship of 26 oars (a levy ship, from about 900)
ships.period_name: ON snekkja; OE snacc (?)
ships.cultures_note: english and frisian: the ship a district owes its king (the levy of 1008; the rowed heerkogge) (?)
ships.rowing_sprint: 5 kn for a quarter of an hour, then 3.5 to 4 kn (Helge Ask) [VSM-Trips]
evidence: Skuldelev 5, about 1030, Denmark: 17.3 x 2.5 x 0.6 m, displaces 7.8 t, 26 oars, about 30 men, sail 46 m2; built partly of reused timber: a levy ship kept going cheaply [VSM-S5] [CP]
Ladby (Funen), 900-950: about 22 x 3 x 0.5 m, 16 pairs of oars [da-Ladby]
With 13 benches, that is, 26 oarsmen, a snekke was regarded as the smallest ship usable for warfare [WP-Long]

Helge Ask trials: 5 to 6 kn kept up in 5 to 10 m/s on or abaft the beam; 2 kn at best to windward; 3.5 to 4 kn rowed, 5 kn in a sprint; she capsized in 1993 tacking in a gusting wind [VSM-Trials] [VSM-Trips]
ships.look: Long, very narrow and low, thirteen oar ports a side, patched planking; a modest mast and sail.
uncertain: whether a merchant ever held one: the levy fell on districts and great men (?)
cargo 1 t (D)
the max of 15 kn is the museum's estimate
ships.built_at_note: built on a king's or a shire's order, not for sale
ships.can_go_note: open sea in fair weather: about 1.5 m of sea, and gusts are her danger. Up any river under oars; she beaches anywhere.
ships.what_it_is: The smallest ship fit for war: seventeen metres, twenty-six oars, thirty men and almost no cargo. A house holds one only as a duty or an honour, when a king or a shire lays a ship on it.
ships.why_want_it: She is rank and safety, not trade: an escort that catches any raider in light air and carries the house's name to a king's muster.
judged: that the player can hold her at all: a reward of stage 5 (the name), with the levy of 1008 as the hook (?)
cost 2400 d: derived 2,000 to 2,700 d; the real cost is thirty men
crew_min 14: half the oars (D)
